Adult Deep-water Cape hake (Merluccius paradoxus) commonly reach a body mass of 12,540 grams [Wwi = 12,540 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships based on captured specimens. This maximum recorded wet weight corresponds to an ultimate total length of 115 centimeters [Li = 115 centimeters], making this species one of the larger gadiform fishes inhabiting the continental slope of southern Africa. Females exhibit pronounced size dimorphism, with the largest individuals consistently being gravid females collected during research trawl surveys. The length-weight relationship used to estimate asymptotic mass was parameterised from a comprehensive dataset spanning multiple decades, providing a robust characterisation of somatic growth in this commercially valuable, slow-growing demersal species. These morphometric benchmarks are essential for fisheries stock assessment models that rely on accurate maximum size estimates to calculate yield-per-recruit and spawning biomass ratios under current harvesting regimes.

Neonatal mass in Merluccius paradoxus is exceedingly low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth reflects the small egg diameter of approximately 900 micrometres, typical of batch-spawning teleosts that produce large numbers of pelagic eggs. The buoyant, transparent eggs drift in the upper water column, where the endotrophic larvae undergo rapid yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding at first mouth opening. Such a low initial mass imposes a narrow window for successful larval feeding, as the point of no return is reached within days if suitable planktonic prey is not encountered. The energetic constraints acting during this lecithotrophic phase are critical in determining early survival rates and subsequent recruitment variability in this species.

Female Merluccius paradoxus reach sexual maturity at a total length of 47.8 centimeters [Lp = 47.8 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 825 grams [Wwp = approximately 825 grams]. This size at maturation is notably smaller than the ultimate body size, indicating a substantial post-pubertal growth phase during which females continue somatic expansion while initiating reproductive investment. Histological examination of ovarian tissue indicates that vitellogenesis onset and first gonadal recrudescence become evident once individuals exceed this length. The ratio of length at puberty to asymptotic length is consistent with values reported for other iteroparous gadoids inhabiting cool-temperate waters. This relatively delayed maturation is thought to buffer against sporadic recruitment failures by ensuring that reproductive females attain a body size sufficient to produce multiple, high-volume egg batches across successive spawning seasons.

The maximum reproductive output of Merluccius paradoxus has been characterised under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce approximately 700,000 eggs per spawning event [Ri = approximately 700,000 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning period each year. This annual egg production estimate is based on comparative data from the congeneric silver hake Merluccius bilinearis, which exhibits similar batch fecundity at analogous temperatures. The sustained high reproductive rate at 7.5 °C reflects the species adaptation to the relatively cold, stable waters of the Benguela Current system, where prolonged spawning seasons allow for considerable annual egg production. Such elevated fecundity compensates for the high larval mortality typical of pelagic early life stages.
